newsitem.title: UK: UK business group warns against tax, rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK business group warns against tax, rate cuts.

text.p: A leading British business group urged finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Thursday to leave interest rates on hold and not to cut taxes in his last pre-election budget next month.

Echoing calls from the Confederation of British Industry last month, the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said tampering with either interest rates or taxes could upset the delicate balance of economic recovery.

"This is the last BCC economic survey before the budget and it indicates plainly that the Chancellor and the Bank of England must leave interest rates and taxes alone," Ian Peters, deputy director-general of the organisation, said.
"Further reductions could cause undue stimulus to the economy whilst any increase could threaten the delicate balance of this recovery and hurt export markets."

Earlier this week BOE governor Eddie George has also warned Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to resist the temptation to trim taxes in his November 26 budget. He has also been pressing for an interest rate rise to stem emerging inflation pressures.
But Clarke is widely expected to cut income tax in the budget to to help boost the ailing Conservative government's chances of winning a general election due by next May.
He has cut official interest rates four times since last December, over-ruling the objections of the Bank of England on the last occasion in June.

The BCC's third quarter economic survey showed an improving economic climate in Britain, with consumer demand continuing to drive service sector sales forward. The benefit of this was now clearly being felt in the manufacturing sector.
"This survey is particularly encouraging," Peters said. "The economy continues to grow at a steady rate and the manufacturing sector is returning to levels of confidence last seen 18 months ago."
Large firms in particular had reported an improving business environment and had now seen two months of surging growth.
The improvement in orders and sales has been mirrored in employment intentions, the survey said,

Service sector firms reported a small improvement in jobs growth while the manufacturing sector was seeing significant increases in employment expectations. Large manufacturing firms were no longer net shedders of jobs.
Export activity remained very stable, with both manufacturers and service firms seeing sales growing at a similar level to the second quarter.
This suggested that the rise in the pound and subdued demand in some European markets were not having too adverse an effect on exports, the BCC said.
